A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DC-FW research, with matching authors, problem formulation, core algorithm, and retained experiments. All 16 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original QAPLIB experiments and CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 neural-network training results, including an appendix analysis of constraint-radius sensitivity.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds partially observed embedding alignment, repeated QAP comparisons, and a numerical illustration of stationarity measures.

M1.justification: The two-loop DC-FW solver, smooth decompositions, and adaptive tolerance strategy remain. Equation (2) now explicitly uses an arbitrary subgradient for nonsmooth g, and Section 5 develops conditional and proximal subgradient specializations. These are limited adaptations of the existing framework; the additional QAP variants instantiate decompositions already present in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds English-French word-embedding alignment with partially observed target embeddings, introducing a distinct language domain and nonsmooth optimization task. QAPLIB and both CIFAR classification datasets remain; the neural-network experiments move to Appendix C rather than being removed.

E2.justification: The added QAP comparison evaluates nonconvex CGS from Qu et al. alongside FW and three DC-FW variants. The new alignment experiment evaluates FW-K from Khamaru and Wainwright and FW-M from Millán et al.; fully observed Procrustes supplies an additional quality reference. v1's experiments compared against standard or stochastic FW.

E3.justification: The new alignment protocol uses 300-dimensional embeddings, 10,000 words, observation probability 0.1, regularization 10^-4, and initialization at zero, evaluating FW gap against iterations, SVD computations, and runtime. Appendix B adds a 10-hour stopping cap and an adapted CGS tolerance strategy for its additional QAP comparison. The retained main QAP and neural-network settings are substantially unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix B newly compares three DC decompositions on QAP, directly testing whether decomposition choice affects solution quality. Section 4 and Figure 1 add a numerical case study comparing projected-gradient and proximal-point measures around different stationary points. The earlier neural-network constraint-radius sensitivity analysis is retained.

E5.justification: v2's additional QAP comparison reports ten Monte Carlo instances per method and dataset, with means and 90% confidence intervals in Figure 4. v1 provides no corresponding repeated-run counts or uncertainty intervals. This is new statistical reporting, without establishing that the original main-text experiment used fewer runs.

E6.justification: New results include DC-FW variant 1 beating CGS on 68.7 QAP instances on average, versus 46.4 in the reverse comparison. Alignment results report 88 DC-FW subgradient calls versus 10,000 for FW-K/FW-M, and 93.11% of fully observed Procrustes alignment quality. These are added experiments; the original QAP summary remains 73 wins, 43 losses, 18 ties, and mean errors 0.0085 versus 0.0112.

T1.justification: Definition 1 now minimizes over the subdifferential, and Lemma 1 adds a formal critical-point characterization with a proof in Appendix A. Corollary 6 extends the strongly convex-set result beyond the earlier smooth CGS specialization, while Section 5 states nonsmooth oracle guarantees. The proximal-point lemma also changes from claiming equality with the DC gap to an upper-bound relationship.

C1.justification: The headline framework and O(1/epsilon^2), O(1/epsilon), and strongly convex-set complexity claims remain. The abstract broadens the empirical comparison from standard FW to other projection-free algorithms, and the introduction/conclusion replace neural-network training with partially observed alignment in their highlighted experimental contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of decomposition-dependent gap geometry and curvature retention, qualifies criticality versus stationarity for nonsmooth problems, and explains alignment runtime differences through oracle costs. It also warns that FW-M backtracking can fail with inaccurate objective evaluations. The existing limitation concerning unproved stochastic extensions remains.

D1.justification: v2 supplies gradients and exact line-search derivations for two additional QAP decompositions and documents the added CGS implementation. It specifies full-SVD implementations of the alignment subgradient and linear oracle, together with data dimensions, masking, regularization, and initialization. Existing hardware, software, neural-network architecture, and adaptive-tolerance details are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Khamaru and Wainwright as a close predecessor, substantially expands the comparison with Millán et al., and distinguishes their oracle costs from DC-FW. It also expands the CGS positioning around momentum and stationarity measures, and discusses Pokutta's 2025 work as a subsequent extension. These changes go beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The exposition is substantially reorganized: proofs are collected in Appendix A, strongly convex-set analysis moves into the general framework, a nonsmooth section is introduced, and neural-network experiments and implementation details are consolidated in Appendix C. The motivation, contributions, and related-work narrative are also revised.

P2.justification: v2 adds the stationarity contour illustration, alignment convergence/cost plots, and QAP comparison heatmap with confidence intervals. Existing neural-network plots move to the appendix and are resized with revised axes and legends. The title block, typography, and page layout also change substantially.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central decomposition and oracle-efficiency claims through direct decomposition comparisons, repeated QAP evaluations with confidence intervals, and cost comparisons against closely related methods. It preserves the earlier experiments and clarifies nonsmooth criticality, addressing important weaknesses in v1's support and scope specification. Some inconsistencies remain, including gradient notation in Algorithm 1 despite the subgradient formulation, but the net gains are substantial.
